paras: The lynching at Deming, New Mexico, was the hanging of an unnamed man by a mob of citizens on the evening of Sunday, August 27, 1882, hours after he was jailed for cutting the throat of a Frenchman. Taken from the jail, he was hanged from a telegraph pole by the railroad track and left there until late the next morning. The story ran as a short wire item from Washington to Montana, often under headlines that treated it as rough justice, and none of the reports gave the race of either man.

According to a Deming dispatch dated August 28, the man was a stranger who arrived on Sunday morning, got drunk and went around the streets "in a boisterous way." He took a dislike to a Frenchman and swore to kill him before night. A separate account in the Arizona Weekly Citizen said the two had exchanged words earlier, that others intervened, and that the Frenchman, described as "a good natured fellow," was singing after a drink or two when he passed the stranger again.

Toward evening the stranger drew a knife and cut the Frenchman's throat. In the local account, bystanders had warned him that "tough fellows" in town would not stand for it, and he answered that he was "pretty tough himself." Officers seized him, handcuffed him and lodged him in jail.

A short time later, after the train had left, a mob went to the jail and took the prisoner out. The Arizona Weekly Citizen's local version said the citizens acted when the officer went away, put a lariat around his neck and dragged him over a quarter of a mile. They hanged him from one of the cross pieces of a telegraph pole at the railroad track, and the body was still hanging late on Monday morning.

The same paper reported that a jury was called and that its foreman declared, with all agreeing, that they did not know how the body got there or who put it there. No arrest of any member of the mob, and no name for the lynched man or the Frenchman, appears in the coverage.

Nearly all the coverage came from one source, a Deming special to the Tucson Star relayed by wire on August 28 and 29 and printed in papers including the Alexandria Gazette, the Washington Evening Star, the Sacramento Record-Union and the Lancaster Intelligencer. A shorter wire, run by the Washington Evening Critic and the Wheeling Register, called the victim of the knife attack "an inoffensive Frenchman" and his attacker "the murderer." Several dispatches gave garbled datelines or places, printing "Reming" for Deming or placing the town in Arizona.

Headlines framed the hanging as punishment: the Sacramento Record-Union used "Saving the Courts Trouble," the Seattle Post-Intelligencer "A Little Honest Lynch Law," and the Wheeling Register "Judge Lynch Passes Sentence." The Las Vegas Daily Gazette, in New Mexico, put "DEMING DEVILTRY" on its front page with the line that the desperado "Departs via Telegraph." Eastern news summaries such as the Savannah Morning News reduced it to a sentence among other crimes, saying a "rough" had been "seized by a mob of citizens." Only the Arizona Weekly Citizen added local detail beyond the wire, including the jury's verdict.

The Deming dispatches dated August 28 and later summaries place the events on Sunday, August 27, while the Dillon Tribune said "last Monday" and some wire datelines read August 20 or 24, probably misprints. Most reports called the Frenchman's wound mortal or said he was killed, but the fullest Deming dispatch said only that it would "probably result fatally."

bases: Citizens or a mob took a man accused of cutting a Frenchman's throat from the Deming jail and hanged him from a telegraph pole (A2, A17, A18).

A 'party of citizens' or 'mob' took an untried prisoner from jail and hanged him for the throat-cutting of a Frenchman (A2, A17, A18); headlines such as 'Saving the Courts Trouble' and 'Judge Lynch Passes Sentence' framed it as punishment (A3, A7). None of the reports gives the race of the lynched man or of the Frenchman.

The Tucson Star's Deming special (A2, A3, A5), a separate short wire (A1, A7) and a local narrative in the Arizona Weekly Citizen with details absent from the wire (A18) agree on the throat-cutting, arrest and hanging from a telegraph pole.

framing.detail: Headlines 'Saving the Courts Trouble', 'A Little Honest Lynch Law' and 'Judge Lynch Passes Sentence' presented the hanging as deserved punishment of a 'murderer'.
Most papers ran the Tucson wire under plain headings such as 'Murderer Lynched' and 'Hanged by a Mob'.
The New Mexico Las Vegas Gazette headlined it 'DEMING DEVILTRY' with the jest that the desperado 'Departs via Telegraph'.

versions.value: Sunday, August 27 ('yesterday' in a special dated the 28th; 'the 27th instant')

conflicts.note: The Deming dispatches dated the 28th, which describe Sunday events, are the closest sources; the Aug. 20 and Aug. 24 datelines in papers printed Aug. 29-30 look like OCR or typesetting errors, and the later 'yesterday' repeats a relayed wire.
The Deming specials and the New Mexico paper (A9) place it in New Mexico; the Arizona placements come from distant papers.
No report confirms the Frenchman's death.
